summary: This RFC is the official specification of the NICNAME/WHOIS protocol and service, which lets users look up information about people and hosts. It updates RFC 812 and was replaced by RFC 3912.

plainLanguage.summary: NICNAME/WHOIS lets a user query a network directory for information about registered users, mailboxes, organizations, and hosts. The client sends a single line to TCP port 43 and receives a human-readable response.

questions: what is the nicname whois protocol
how did early whois search commands work
subtitle: The NICNAME/WHOIS query protocol uses TCP port 43 and human-readable replies.

tldr.problem: Internet users needed to look up people, mailboxes, organizations, and hosts in the NIC database.
tldr.mechanism: A client connects to TCP port 43, sends one command line ending in CRLF, receives a response, and the server closes the connection.
tldr.outcome: RFC 954 obsoletes RFC 812 and was later obsoleted by RFC 3912.

today: RFC 954 is obsoleted by RFC 3912. It had obsoleted RFC 812.

sections.title: The NICNAME/WHOIS Service
sections.content:
The NICNAME/WHOIS server provides a network directory service from the SRI-NIC machine. It returns information such as a registered user's name, U.S. mailing address, telephone number, and network mailbox.

The database can also provide information about organizations, DDN nodes and associated hosts, and TAC telephone numbers. Responses are formatted for people to read.
sections.plainLanguage: The service searches a directory of registered people and network entities. Its replies are intended to be read by a person.

sections.title: The Query Exchange
sections.content:
A user connects to the SRI-NIC service host at TCP port 43. The client sends one command line ending with CRLF and receives a response; the server closes the connection when output is complete.

NICNAME is the global name for the user program, though many sites called it WHOIS. Programs pass their single argument directly to the server.
sections.plainLanguage: The client opens a TCP connection to port 43, sends one line, and reads the result. The server closes the connection after sending the response.

sections.title: Command Lines and Replies
sections.content:
A command line normally contains a single name specification. A line containing only a question mark asks the server to list the available search formats. A leading period forces a name-only search, while an exclamation point forces a handle-only search.

Mailbox searches can use forms such as Smith@, @Host, and Smith@Host. A leading asterisk requests a group's or host's membership list. The RFC says the response formats are not intended to be machine-readable.
sections.plainLanguage: Users can search names, handles, or mailboxes using different command forms. A question mark asks the server to explain the formats it accepts.

sections.title: Who the Database Covered
sections.content:
The DCA requested registration for individuals with directories on ARPANET or MILNET hosts who could pass traffic across the DoD Internet. MILNET TAC users were required to be registered.

To register, a user sent a full name, mailing address, telephone number, and one network mailbox to the NIC registrar by electronic mail.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo describes who was requested to register and which details to send. These included a name, postal address, telephone number, and network mailbox.

references.text: Harrenstien, K. and V. White, "NICNAME/WHOIS", RFC 812, March 1982.
